ready1_open_rewrite.raw_question_text:
We consider a $5 \times 5$ square that is split up into 25 fields. Initially all fields are white. In each move it is allowed to change the colour of two fields that are horizontally or vertically adjacent (i.e. white fields turn black and black ones turn white). What is the smallest number of moves needed to obtain the chessboard colouring shown in the diagram?

ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: On the left in the figure is a 5×5 grid, and all cells are white; an arrow points to the 5×5 grid on the right. The target pattern on the right is an alternating checkerboard coloring, with the upper-left corner still white, and the gray/black cells are exactly the cells satisfying row number + column number being odd: row 1 columns 2 and 4; row 2 columns 1, 3, and 5; row 3 columns 2 and 4; row 4 columns 1, 3, and 5; row 5 columns 2 and 4, for a total of 12 gray/black cells. Reasoning: Regard the 25 cells as the vertices of a 5×5 grid graph. One operation selects one horizontal or vertical adjacent edge, and flips the two endpoints of this edge. If a certain cell is finally black, then it has been flipped an odd number of times; if it is finally white, then it has been flipped an even number of times. Therefore the problem is equivalent to: using the fewest edges so that the odd-degree vertices are exactly the 12 target black cells. The grid graph is a bipartite graph, and the parity of row number + column number of adjacent cells is opposite. The 12 target black cells are all in the same bipartition part, namely the cells whose row number + column number is odd. The length of any path connecting two target black cells must be even; and there are no adjacent target black cells, so connecting any pair of target black cells requires length at least 2. The 12 target black cells must be paired into 6 pairs, so at least 6×2=12 operations are needed. A construction of 12 operations can achieve the target: pair target black cells at distance 2. Horizontal pairing: row 1 c2 and c4, via c3; row 3 c2 and c4, via c3; row 5 c2 and c4, via c3. Vertical pairing: column 1 r2 and r4, via r3; column 3 r2 and r4, via r3; column 5 r2 and r4, via r3. Each pair uses two adjacent flips; the middle cell is flipped twice and remains white, and the two endpoints are each flipped once and become black. In this way there are a total of 6×2=12 operations, and the checkerboard coloring in the figure is obtained. Therefore the lower bound can be reached, and the minimum number of times is 12.

method.method_draft: First read the diagram: the right-hand 5 by 5 board is an alternating chessboard pattern with the top-left square white, so the grey/black target squares are exactly the 12 cells with row+column odd. From the text, each move toggles the two endpoints of one horizontal or vertical adjacency. Model the board as the 5 by 5 grid graph: each cell is a vertex and each allowed move is choosing an edge and toggling its two endpoints. The task is to express the 12 target black vertices as the odd-degree vertices of a minimum-size edge set, i.e. a minimum T-join. Since all 12 target black cells lie in the same bipartition class of the grid, any path pairing two target vertices has even length, and because no two target black cells are adjacent in the diagram, every such path has length at least 2. The 12 target vertices must be paired into 6 pairs, so at least 6·2 = 12 moves are needed. Then give an explicit construction with 12 moves by pairing grey cells at distance 2: for example pair row 1 cells c2-c4 through c3, row 3 cells c2-c4 through c3, row 5 cells c2-c4 through c3, and pair vertically c1 in rows 2 and 4, c3 in rows 2 and 4, c5 in rows 2 and 4. Each pair uses two adjacent-edge toggles, making only the two endpoints black and the middle cell white again. This achieves the shown board in 12 moves, so the minimum is 12.

method.method_draft: First read the diagram: the desired final board has grey/black cells in a checkerboard pattern with top-left white, hence there are 12 final black cells and no two final black cells share an edge. From the text, a move toggles exactly two adjacent cells. For a lower bound, look at the last move that affects each final black cell. Since that cell is black at the end, it must be toggled in some last move. In that last move, the other toggled cell is adjacent to it. But in the target diagram every neighbor of a final black cell is final white, because the black cells are isolated in the checkerboard pattern. Therefore the same move cannot be the last move for two different final black cells: two adjacent cells cannot both be final black. Thus the 12 final black cells require 12 distinct last moves, giving a lower bound of 12 moves. For achievability, explicitly perform 12 moves in 6 two-move chains: connect pairs of intended black cells separated by one white cell, toggling both adjacent dominoes along that length-2 path. Use the three horizontal pairs in rows 1, 3, and 5 between columns 2 and 4, and the three vertical pairs in columns 1, 3, and 5 between rows 2 and 4. Each chain toggles its two target endpoints once and its middle cell twice, leaving the middle white. Hence 12 moves suffice and, by the lower bound, are minimal.

推理如下：每一步只能翻转一对水平或竖直相邻的格子。对每一个最终为黑色的格子，考虑最后一次翻转它的那一步。因为它最后是黑色，所以它必须在某一步中被翻转到黑色。该步同时翻转它的一个相邻格子；但目标棋盘中任意黑格的相邻格都是白格，所以同一步不可能同时作为两个不同最终黑格的“最后一步”。因此 12 个最终黑格至少需要 12 个不同的最后步骤，所以下界是 12 步。

再说明 12 步可以做到。把相隔一个白格的目标黑格两两连接：在第1、3、5行分别对第2列和第4列之间做两步翻转，即翻转 (r,2)-(r,3) 和 (r,3)-(r,4)；这使两端变黑，中间格翻转两次仍为白。再在第1、3、5列分别对第2行和第4行之间做两步翻转，即翻转 (2,c)-(3,c) 和 (3,c)-(4,c)；同样两端变黑，中间格仍为白。这样共有 6 条长度为2的链，每条用 2 步，总共 12 步，正好得到图中的棋盘染色。

再说明 12 步可以做到。把相隔一个白格的目标黑格两两连接：在第1、3、5行分别对第2列和第4列之间做两步翻转，即翻转 (r,2)-(r,3) 和 (r,3)-(r,4)；这使两端变黑，中间格翻转两次仍为白。再在第1、3、5列分别对第2行和第4行之间做两步翻转，即翻转 (2,c)-(3,c) 和 (3,c)-(4,c)；同样两端变黑，中间格仍为白。这样共有 6 条长度为2的链，每条用 2 步，总共 12 步，正好得到图中的棋盘染色。

所以下界可达到，最小步数为 12。

raw_record.original_question: We consider a $5 \times 5$ square that is split up into 25 fields. Initially all fields are white. In each move it is allowed to change the colour of two fields that are horizontally or vertically adjacent (i.e. white fields turn black and black ones turn white). What is the smallest number of moves needed to obtain the chessboard colouring shown in the diagram?
raw_record.final_cot:
Image description: On the left in the figure is a 5×5 grid, and all cells are white; an arrow points to the 5×5 grid on the right. The target pattern on the right is an alternating checkerboard coloring, with the upper-left corner still white, and the gray/black cells are exactly the cells satisfying row number + column number being odd: row 1 columns 2 and 4; row 2 columns 1, 3, and 5; row 3 columns 2 and 4; row 4 columns 1, 3, and 5; row 5 columns 2 and 4, for a total of 12 gray/black cells.

Reasoning: Regard the 25 cells as the vertices of a 5×5 grid graph. One operation selects one horizontal or vertical adjacent edge, and flips the two endpoints of this edge. If a certain cell is finally black, then it has been flipped an odd number of times; if it is finally white, then it has been flipped an even number of times. Therefore the problem is equivalent to: using the fewest edges so that the odd-degree vertices are exactly the 12 target black cells.

The grid graph is a bipartite graph, and the parity of row number + column number of adjacent cells is opposite. The 12 target black cells are all in the same bipartition part, namely the cells whose row number + column number is odd. The length of any path connecting two target black cells must be even; and there are no adjacent target black cells, so connecting any pair of target black cells requires length at least 2. The 12 target black cells must be paired into 6 pairs, so at least 6×2=12 operations are needed.

A construction of 12 operations can achieve the target: pair target black cells at distance 2. Horizontal pairing: row 1 c2 and c4, via c3; row 3 c2 and c4, via c3; row 5 c2 and c4, via c3. Vertical pairing: column 1 r2 and r4, via r3; column 3 r2 and r4, via r3; column 5 r2 and r4, via r3. Each pair uses two adjacent flips; the middle cell is flipped twice and remains white, and the two endpoints are each flipped once and become black. In this way there are a total of 6×2=12 operations, and the checkerboard coloring in the figure is obtained. Therefore the lower bound can be reached, and the minimum number of times is 12.
